articles.title: California diners are cutting back as costs soar — but restaurant owner reveals one trend that's booming
articles.summary: Happy hour business jumped from roughly 8% to nearly 30% of sales at a San Diego restaurant group as California diners hunt for cheaper meals.
articles.body: Happy hour is becoming the main event for some California diners as the state's high cost of living pushes more customers to seek out discounted meals instead of paying full price for a night out. Chef Alex Carballo of Grand Restaurant Group told Fox News Digital that happy hour once accounted for an estimated 5% to 8% of his business. Now, that figure has climbed to nearly 30%, even as customers cut back on dining out. "My happy hour has increased a lot, so I think people are looking for deals and looking for options," Carballo said. The shift reflects a broader affordability squeeze across California where residents told Fox News Digital that rising costs for housing, groceries and gasoline are forcing them to rethink everyday spending. California has the highest overall price levels in the nation, according to 2024 data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, with prices running roughly 11% above the national average. But affordability pressures extend far beyond the Golden State, as Americans nationwide grapple with elevated costs for housing, groceries and other everyday necessities. NEWSOM UNDER FIRE AS CALIFORNIA GAS TAX HIKE SENDS PUMP PRICES EVEN HIGHER Carballo said customers are visiting his restaurants less frequently, with some scaling back how often they eat out. "They're going out three times a week, where they were coming out to see me four or five [times]. And the people that used to see three times a week, they're only coming out once," he said. What was once a stop for drinks or appetizers before dinner is increasingly becoming the dinner itself, Carballo said. "Now it's like, that's where they're going and they're hitting those scenes," he said. Customers can still enjoy the same food, service and atmosphere at lower prices, Carballo said, making happy-hour deals particularly appealing. But those discounts also create challenges for restaurant operators who are already grappling with rising expenses. "I'm still paying the same amount for food. I'm still paying the employees. My rent didn't change. Nothing changed. Only thing I'm doing is trying to discount my product to gain people to come here," Carballo said. AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES Fox News Digital also spoke with residents in Southern California who described making financial trade-offs that extend well beyond restaurants. Jonas, a Santa Monica resident who is planning a wedding with his fiancée, said he and his fiancée are reevaluating their budget as everyday expenses continue to add up. "Certainly gas is expensive, rent is high, and then grocery prices are pretty high as well," Jonas said. He estimated that he spends approximately $100 a week on groceries and said rising costs are influencing their decisions about dining out and transportation. The couple is "eating out a little bit less," Jonas said, adding that he has also started walking to work to "save money on gas as well." "I think that people are just seeing prices go up everywhere, and feeling like they're getting less than what they had four years ago maybe," he said. "I think everybody's really feeling that." BELOVED RESTAURANT CHAIN DWINDLES FROM 850 LOCATIONS TO 87, BUT EXPERT SEES 'A LOT OF LIFE LEFT' For some Californians, the financial strain has gone beyond cutting back on restaurants. Justin, a California native from Glendora who moved to Las Vegas seven years ago, told Fox News Digital that the state's high cost of living was one of the reasons he left. "Affordability is crazy," Justin said while visiting Los Angeles for a Rams game. "I left seven years ago and I thought gas and you know rent was high then," he said. "Here I am seven years later and it's ... one of the reasons why I'm in Vegas now. It's just unaffordable." Justin said many of his friends who remain in California are still struggling with housing costs. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKID ROW "90% of my friends are living with a roommate. It is really hard to live alone here," he said. Housing remains another major affordability challenge in the Golden State. Just 19% of California households could afford the state's median-priced home of $916,750 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the California Association of Realtors. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In Venice, resident Tatiana described rising expenses across everything from gasoline to groceries and neighborhood restaurants. "Everything is more expensive, gas is more expensive, food," she told Fox News Digital. "There's really very few affordable restaurants left on Abbot Kinney. Even our local co-op prices have gone up at least 15%. Everything costs more." "We're not getting any breaks in California," she said.

articles.title: Joy Behar wants Trump back on ‘The View’ despite saying he’s ‘not long for this world’
articles.summary: Joy Behar invited Trump back to "The View" while claiming he's "not long for this world," prompting a sharp response from the White House team.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Joy Behar extended an unlikely invitation Friday to her longtime political foe President Donald Trump, saying she would welcome him back to the daytime talk show despite suggesting that he is "not long for this world." Behar, who has said she wants her legacy to include helping remove Trump from office, reflected on her decades-long history with the president during an interview with New York Magazine. "I’d love Donald Trump to take the heat," said the longtime Trump critic. "You know Trump is not long for this world. He seems ill. He does not seem like he’s well," Behar added. BILL MAHER REVEALS HE'S HAVING DINNER WITH TRUMP AGAIN, SAYS HE WAS 'REALLY NICE' BY TEXT A White House spokesperson responded to Behar’s comments about Trump’s well-being in a statement to Fox News Digital. "‘Joyless’ Behar is an extremely unlikeable, talentless hack with a poorly rated TV show who clearly suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome," the statement said. "I lose braincells every single time I have the displeasure of hearing her speak," the spokesperson continued. TRUMP DECLARED 'FULLY FIT' FOR ALL PRESIDENTIAL DUTIES AFTER ANNUAL PHYSICAL SHOWS 'EXCELLENT HEALTH' Behar’s comments mark the latest instance in which "The View" co-host has publicly questioned Trump’s health. Last month, she argued that the media does not scrutinize Trump’s health to the same degree it scrutinized former President Joe Biden’s. Despite their bitter political divide today, Behar and Trump share a history from long before his political career. Trump made more than a dozen appearances on "The View" before he was president and Behar even attended his wedding to Marla Maples at The Plaza Hotel in 1993. DONALD TRUMP'S AGE IS NOT RECEIVING THE SAME 'SCRUTINY' AS BIDEN'S DID, ATLANTIC WRITER COMPLAINS Behar said Trump’s humor has changed significantly since she knew him as a New York celebrity decades ago. "I knew him when he was just an annoying New York figure," she said. "Back then, he had a sense of humor that was not as bizarre as it is now. Now his sense of humor is making fun of handicapped people." "The View" co-host recalled her earlier interactions with Trump, including a time in which she compared Trump to Woody Allen after he said that he would date his daughter Ivanka if they were not related. "He actually thought that was funny," Behar said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Behar has said that Trump is "much more dangerous" now than he was during his first term and recently urged Americans to call on their members of Congress to invoke the 25th Amendment against him because she believes he is "destroying the United States of America."

articles.title: Blackburn on AI Kendrick Lamar clip backlash: It wasn’t ‘intended to offend’
articles.summary: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) is defending herself after coming under fire for sharing a video, which seemed to be AI-generated, in which she appeared in the place of rapper Kendrick Lamar during his 2025 Super Bowl LIX Halftime Show performance. In a clip Fox 13 Memphis’ Rob Sneed posted to Instagram Friday, the reporter asked…
articles.body:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) is defending herself after coming under fire for sharing a video , which seemed to be AI-generated, in which she appeared in the place of rapper Kendrick Lamar during his 2025 Super Bowl LIX Halftime Show performance.

In a clip Fox 13 Memphis’ Rob Sneed posted to Instagram Friday, the reporter asked Blackburn about the viral moment, to which the lawmaker responded saying someone else had made the original video, and her campaign team shared it because she thought it was “fun.”

“It was a video that a county commissioner had created, and I thought it was just something that was fun,” Blackburn said.

Blackburn faced criticism online for sharing the likely AI-generated video, showing her dancing to Lamar’s popular song, “Not Like Us” — which he performed during the Super Bowl. Other Tennessee politicians appear as her background dancers, including Rep. Tim Burchett (R) and Sen. Bill Haggerty (R).

As of Saturday afternoon, the video has over 2.2 million views on social platform X.

Commenters generally responded negatively to the video, including former Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.), who said, “Boomer thinks AI makes her look cool.” Other users simply called the video “cringe.”

The Tennessee senator has advocated against AI deepfake videos in the past, and she introduced a bill to protect the likeness of creators from being used without their consent.

Sneed also pressed Blackburn on another concern surrounding the video: that it could have offended Black Americans. The song, which famously includes disses against fellow rapper Drake, is often interpreted as a commentary on the appropriation of Black artists’ work.

“There would never be any action that was intended to offend,” Blackburn responded.

Blackburn is running for Tennessee governor against Democrat Jerri Green. Green responded to her opponent’s video on X.

“When I say please stop using AI to support our campaign, this is what I mean…,” Green wrote.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Blackburn a 94 percent chance to win Tennessee gubernatorial race. The state has not elected a Democrat to serve as its governor since 2006.
